3qmzqs: A fact or not yet: the idea of the subjunctive
17pvv3g: The **indicative** presents information as a fact: something that is, that happens or that you know. The **subjunctive** presents an action that is **not a fact** yet: something you wish for, ask for or aim at for another person.

1e1r4x3: That is why the subjunctive almost always comes after a verb of wishing, requesting or purpose, and almost always after **que**. With **para que** you express the goal for another person: _Te dejo la llave para que abras tú_.

1j6gom9: Irregular verbs: the yo stem and the six special ones
b1omv9: Many irregular verbs **keep the yo irregularity** in all persons: _tengo_ → _tenga, tengas, tengamos_; _hago_ → _haga_; _conozco_ → _conozca_; _salgo_ → _salga_; _digo_ → _diga_; _pongo_ → _ponga_.
53r45r: Stem-changing verbs (**e → ie**, **o → ue**) change in every person except nosotros and vosotros: _quiera, quieras… queramos_; _pueda… podamos_. -ir verbs like **pedir** also close the vowel in nosotros: _pida, pidamos_; **dormir** gives _duerma, durmamos_.
16v3gc1: Six verbs don't follow the yo rule and have to be memorised: **ser** (sea), **estar** (esté), **ir** (vaya), **haber** (haya), **saber** (sepa) and **dar** (dé). And watch the spelling: _buscar_ → _busque_, _llegar_ → _llegue_, _empezar_ → _empiece_.

2ynr4u: **Esperar** works the same way: _Espero llegar a tiempo_ / _Espero que llegues a tiempo_. **Desear** is more formal or more intense: it appears in cards, speeches and written messages.

33pch1: To say goodbye or congratulate someone, Spanish uses short phrases with **¡Que + subjunctive!**: they are the second half of _espero que…_ or _deseo que…_. The most frequent: _¡Que te vaya bien!, ¡Que tengas suerte!, ¡Que lo pases bien!, ¡Que te mejores!, ¡Que disfrutes!_

13sxok9: In the subjunctive, a single vowel often decides the meaning: _Sé que Camila **habla** con los vecinos_ (a fact) and _Quiero que Camila **hable** con los vecinos_ (a wish). If you don't pronounce the last vowel clearly, your listener won't know what you mean.
1clcnmp: Spanish vowels are short and tense: don't lengthen them or turn them into a neutral sound at the end of the word. Say **-e** with your mouth slightly open and your lips spread; **-a**, with your mouth wide open.
jw2q2l: Also be careful with **esté** (es-TÉ, subjunctive of estar) and **este** (ES-te, demonstrative). The accent marks the stress and changes the word.

dqe27g: Next Saturday La Taza de Papel opens its doors on 57th Street: a bookshop with a café that Camila Rojas, a 34-year-old engineer, has spent almost two years preparing. «I want people to come and read without hurrying and for nobody to tell them they have to order something to stay», she explains while placing novels on a shelf made of recycled wood.
yd9mlg: The premises used to be an old stationery shop. Camila kept the original counter and decorated the walls with old photos of the neighbourhood lent to her by the neighbours. «I don't expect to get rich», she says, laughing. «I hope the business will be sustainable and that we can run writing workshops for children on Saturday mornings.»
1fu03tb: The neighbours have already left their messages in a notebook by the door. Don Hernando, who has been selling fruit on the corner for thirty years, wrote: «I hope it goes very well for you and I hope you sell lots of books, but don't put up the price of the coffee». A student signed with a drawing and a sentence: «May the wifi never fail». And the owner of the bakery opposite left a practical note: «If you'd like me to bring you fresh bread in the mornings, let me know».
